new_statements.quote: There is grammatical stress in the language which distinguishes between the 1. and 3. person sg. and pl. In order to mark the 1. person stress goes on the first syllable, elsewhere it follows the rules of predictable stress. Examples: tákanina 'we will eat' takanina 'they ate'. Stress is realized as high pitch and length. Except for grammatical usage stress can be predicted on all words according to the following rules: 1) Stress goes to the second last syllable. 2) If the last syllable has a CVC pattern, stress goes to the last syllable but does not lengthen the vowel.
new_statements.citation: Knauber, Martin. 2001. Dawawa Organised Phonology Data. Ms., SIL-PNG (Ukarumpa), 4 pp. SIL Language & Culture Archives entry 42469. https://www.sil.org/resources/archives/42469 (PDF: https://www.sil.org/system/files/reapdata/16/85/73/168573804084911762543001344657508402723/, fetched sources via Wayback snapshot 20240818134812).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default word stress is penultimate; if the word ends in a closed (CVC) syllable, stress falls on that final syllable instead (final closed syllables attract stress; the stressed vowel is then not lengthened). Superimposed on this is a morphological pattern: 1st-person verb forms carry stress on the word-initial syllable, contrasting with otherwise segmentally identical 3rd-person forms (tákanina 'we will eat' vs takanina 'they ate'). Stress is realized as high pitch plus vowel length.
new_statements.exceptions: Grammatical (morphological) initial stress marking 1st person sg./pl. vs 3rd person on verbs; final stress when the last syllable is CVC (closed syllables are rare: tam 'you', bembem 'beans', ebom 'hello', gun 'mat'). Orthography marks stress only on the 1st-person forms.
new_statements.domain_note: Stated for 'all words' (word domain, citation forms); the 4-page OPD gives no discussion of phrase-level prosody. Author reports 12 years of work in the language.
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD describes Dawawa [dww] of Rabaraba district, Milne Bay Province (villages Boya-Boya, Gadovisu, Wanama, Didia, Pova, Manubada), i.e. the language-level glottocode dawa1242 itself; the author notes /j/~[l] free variation 'in one dialect' but does not name dialects. Lithgow 1976 lists the language as 'Dawawa (Mia-i-topa)' in his Kakabai family.

sources.note: p.3 'Suprasegmentals': stress = high pitch + length; predictable: (1) penultimate syllable, (2) final syllable if it is CVC (without vowel lengthening); grammatical stress on the first syllable marks 1st person vs 3rd person (tákanina 'we will eat' vs takanina 'they ate'); orthography marks stress only on 1st-person forms.

sources.citation: Lithgow, David R. 1976. Austronesian languages: Milne Bay and adjacent islands (Milne Bay Province). In S.A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea Area Languages and Language Study vol. 2, 441-523. Pacific Linguistics C-39. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Sec. 8.4 'Stress' (p.475) is an area-wide remark for Papuan Tip Cluster languages (vowel lengthening near word end; stress phonemic in Kilivila, Muyuw, Budibud, Misima; stress predictable within word classes and shifts one syllable rightward under suffixation); nothing specific to Dawawa. Dawawa appears only in classification, cognate percentages, the note on a [ts] phone, and morphology tables.
